newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - AEA eyes weapons disposal work.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - AEA eyes weapons disposal work.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent

Britain's AEA Technology Plc hopes to win business disposing of dangerous weapons stockpiles in Russia, the United States, Europe and China, thanks to the Chemical Weapons Convention that comes into force on Tuesday.

AEA's head of process technology, Bill Batey, said in an interview that the company hoped to win contracts worth tens of millions of pounds with a process first developed to clean up waste from the nuclear reprocessing industry.

The treaty, which passed a major hurdle on April 24 when the U.S. Senate ratified it, bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. The signatories have the declared ambition of ridding the world of chemical weapons within 10 years.
AEA Technology said its "Silver II" process can safely destroy chemical warfare agents.

This technology breaks down the chemical weapons into carbon dioxide, water and inorganic salts, which can be safely vented to the atmosphere, recycled within the plant, or disposed of as standard industrial waste.
Batey said the process had been successfully demonstrated to the U.S. military authorities, disposing of VX chemical agent and mustard gas.
AEA failed to win initial U.S. contracts, but still hopes for business there.

U.S. authorities have so far opted for a process known as neutralisation, which breaks down the chemical agent and allows the residue to be diluted with water. AEA says this results in much higher volumes of waste.
Silver II can also dispose of conventional explosives, and AEA hopes to win its first business with Russia.

"We are negotiating with the Russians. They have major problems with conventional explosives, and they seem very interested. My guess is this will be our first contract. But we haven't been able to interest them in chemical weapons disposal," Batey said.
Experts reckon that Russia has around 45,000 tonnes of chemical weapons, and the Americans about 30,000 tonnes.
About 60 countries have chemical weapons disposal problems, according to Batey.

"In China and Manchuria, leftover from the Sino-Japanese war (in the 1930s), there are a million rounds of chemical weapons in various areas. There have been about 2,000 casualties so far in handling this. I understand Japan has agreed to pay for the disposal; we're looking into that market also."
"There are about 15,000 tonnes in Germany left over from the First World War; they keep finding weapons, and they can't incinerate them any more."
"There's about 15,000 tonnes in Belgium, also from World War One, and what the French have I've got no idea. But they had many major battlefields in the First World War."
Batey said that although no sales had been made yet, he was confident of a major success. "Business could be worth tens of millions of pounds," he said.
AEA Technology was a part of Britain's state-owned Atomic Energy Authority but was privatised last year.
